fields.title: Jonah
fields.subtitle: Yonah, “Dove”
fields.description: The story of a prophet who ran from God. Sent to Nineveh, the great city of Israel’s enemy Assyria, Jonah takes ship for Tarshish instead; the LORD hurls a great wind onto the sea, the sailors throw him overboard, and a great fish swallows him and gives him back. From inside the fish he prays, “It is the LORD who saves.” Then Nineveh hears five words of warning and repents, from the king to the cattle, God relents, and Jonah sits outside the city furious that God is so merciful, until a plant, a worm and a hot east wind teach him otherwise. It ends with a question for every reader. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Jonah?
qa.answer: The fifth of the twelve shorter prophetic books, and the only one that is almost entirely a story about the prophet rather than a collection of his messages. In four chapters God sends Jonah to warn Nineveh, Jonah runs away by sea and is swallowed by a great fish (chapters 1–2), then preaches in Nineveh, which repents and is spared (chapter 3), and finally argues with God about his mercy (chapter 4). It ends with God’s question: “should I not take pity on Nineveh, that great city?” (4:11).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Jonah, and when?
qa.answer: The book does not name its author, and it tells its story about Jonah rather than in his voice. Its hero is the prophet Jonah son of Amittai from Gath-hepher, who 2 Kings 14:25 says prophesied in the reign of Jeroboam II of Israel, in the eighth century BC. Some readers think the book was written in or near Jonah’s own time; many scholars date it later, after the exile, on the grounds of its language and themes. Its message does not depend on settling the date.

qa.question: Why did Jonah run away from God?
qa.answer: The book saves the answer until chapter 4. When Nineveh repents and God spares it, Jonah prays: “That is why I hurried to run away to Tarshish. For I knew that you are a God of grace and tender compassion, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love, and one who relents from sending disaster” (4:2). Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, the cruel empire that threatened Israel, and Jonah did not want God to show mercy to Israel’s enemy.

qa.question: Was Jonah swallowed by a whale?
qa.answer: The Hebrew says “a great fish”, and so does this translation; “whale” comes from older English versions of Jesus’s words in Matthew 12:40. Christians read the story in different ways. Many take it as an account of real events, pointing to the historical Jonah of 2 Kings and to Jesus’s words about Jonah and the people of Nineveh; others read it as an inspired teaching story built around a real prophet, pointing to its artful shape and its open ending. Both readings receive it as Scripture, and both agree that the fish is not the point: it fills three verses, and the book is about the mercy of God.

qa.question: What is the sign of Jonah?
qa.answer: When some of his hearers demanded a sign, Jesus said that the only sign they would be given was “the sign of Jonah the prophet” (Matthew 12:39). He explained that as Jonah spent three days and three nights inside the great sea creature, so the Son of Man would spend three days and three nights in the earth, pointing to his death and resurrection. He added that the people of Nineveh, who repented when Jonah preached, would condemn a generation that did not repent, “Yet here is something greater than Jonah” (Matthew 12:41; compare Luke 11:29–32).

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
He prayed to the LORD, “Please, LORD, did I not say this while I was still in my own country? That is why I hurried to run away to Tarshish. For I knew that you are a God of grace and tender compassion, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love, and one who relents from sending disaster.

— Jonah 4:2

Jonah is the one prophetic book that is almost entirely a story. The other prophets give us their sermons; Jonah gives us one sentence of preaching, five words in Hebrew, and four chapters about the preacher. And the preacher is not a hero. He runs from God, sleeps through a storm, sulks when his message succeeds, and is still arguing with God when the book ends.

Everyone knows the fish. But the fish is not the heart of the story; it occupies three verses. The heart of the story is the verse above, in which a prophet complains to God that he is too merciful. Jonah knew exactly who God was. That was his problem.

Who was Jonah?

Jonah son of Amittai appears only once elsewhere in the Old Testament. The second book of Kings tells how King Jeroboam II of Israel restored Israel’s borders, in the eighth century before Christ, “by the word of the LORD the God of Israel, which he had spoken through his servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.” Gath-hepher was a village in Galilee. So Jonah was a prophet of good news for Israel, a patriot whose word had come true in the expansion of his nation.

Nineveh was a great city of Assyria, the empire that would destroy the northern kingdom of Israel within a few decades and was already feared across the Near East for its cruelty. Its kings boasted in their inscriptions of the cities they burned and the prisoners they impaled and flayed. The prophet Nahum would later call Nineveh “the city of bloodshed”. To be sent there with a warning was to be sent to the enemy, and Jonah understood at once that a warning might mean a chance to repent.

Running away

The word of the LORD comes to Jonah: “Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, because their wickedness has come up before me.” Nineveh lay hundreds of miles to the east. Jonah gets up and goes west, to the port of Joppa, and buys a passage to Tarshish, a city at the far end of the Mediterranean, the edge of the known world. The story is told with a steady downward motion. Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the hold, where he lies down and falls into a deep sleep. Later he will go down to the roots of the mountains.

But “the LORD hurled a great wind onto the sea”, and the ship is about to break apart. The pagan sailors pray, each to his own god, and throw the cargo overboard, while the prophet of the LORD sleeps. It is the captain who has to wake him and tell him to pray. When the lot falls on Jonah, he makes a confession of faith that condemns him out of his own mouth:

He answered them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”

— Jonah 1:9

He fears the God who made the sea, and he is running from him across it. The sailors understand the absurdity better than he does: “What is this that you have done?” Jonah tells them to throw him overboard. They try instead to row to shore; they pray not to be held guilty of his blood; only then do they hurl him into the sea, and it grows calm. Watch what happens to the sailors as the chapter goes on. At first they are “terrified”; then “seized with great fear”; at the end they are “filled with great fear of the LORD”, offering sacrifices and making vows. Jonah has not preached to them at all, and the first converts in his book are already on their knees.

From deep in Sheol

But the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was inside the fish for three days and three nights.

— Jonah 1:17

The fish is not a punishment but a rescue. Jonah, sinking to his death, is swallowed and kept alive, and from inside the fish he prays. His prayer, in chapter 2, is a psalm of thanksgiving, full of the language of the Psalms: the waters closing over him, the seaweed wrapped around his head, the bars of the earth closing behind him, and then, “But you brought my life up from the pit, LORD my God.” It ends with a line that sums up the whole book:

But I will sacrifice to you with a song of thanksgiving; what I have vowed I will make good. It is the LORD who saves.”

— Jonah 2:9

There is a faint irony in the prayer. Jonah says that “Those who devote themselves to useless idols abandon their loyal love”, while above him the pagan sailors he left behind are worshipping the LORD. But the prayer is real, and God hears it. He speaks to the fish, and the fish obeys at once, as everything in this book obeys God except his prophet.

“Forty more days”

Then comes the most important phrase in the book: “The word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time”. God gives second chances to prophets, and the rest of the story will show that he gives them to cities too.

This time Jonah goes. Nineveh is “an exceedingly great city, a three days’ walk across”, and he walks one day into it and delivers his message: “Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown!” He gives no reason and offers no hope. And the impossible happens:

The people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least of them.

— Jonah 3:5

The king himself rises from his throne, lays aside his robe and sits in ashes. He decrees a fast for people and animals alike, and calls everyone to “turn from their evil ways and from the violence they do.” His reasoning is humble and uncertain: “Who knows? God may yet turn and change his mind”. He has no promise to stand on. He simply throws his city on the mercy of a God he does not know. And God sees, and relents, and does not do it.

“Are you right to be angry?”

Any other prophet would have rejoiced. Jonah is furious. Now we learn why he ran in the first place: he knew that God is “a God of grace and tender compassion, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love, and one who relents from sending disaster.” These are the words the LORD himself proclaimed to Moses on Mount Sinai, Israel’s most treasured confession of who God is. Jonah throws them back at God as an accusation. He would rather die than live in a world where God is that merciful to Nineveh.

God answers with a question, “Are you right to be angry?”, and then with an object lesson. Jonah sits east of the city to see what will happen, and God appoints a leafy plant to shade him, and Jonah is overjoyed. Then God appoints a worm to kill the plant and a scorching east wind, and Jonah begs to die again. “Are you right to be angry about the plant?” “I am right to be angry,” he says, “angry enough to die!”

And the book ends with God’s reply, the last question in it:

Then the LORD said, “You took pity on the plant, though you did not work for it or make it grow. It sprang up in a night and died in a night. And should I not take pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 people in it who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals as well?”

— Jonah 4:10–11

There is no answer from Jonah. The story stops there, with the question hanging in the air, and that is deliberate. The reader is left in Jonah’s place, under the withered plant, looking at the city, and must answer for himself.

A book about mercy

Jonah is a book about the reach of God’s mercy, and about how much we resent it when it reaches people we think do not deserve it. Every pagan in the book, the sailors, the king, the people, even the animals in their sackcloth, turns toward God more readily than his prophet does. Jonah cared more for a plant that gave him shade than for a city of a hundred and twenty thousand people. God cares even for the animals.

It is also a book about grace to Jonah himself. God does not abandon his runaway prophet. He sends a storm to stop him, a fish to save him, a second call to recommission him, a plant to shade him, and patient questions to reason with him. The same compassion that Jonah resents for Nineveh is shown to him on every page.

The sign of Jonah

When some of his hearers asked Jesus for a sign, he told them that the only sign they would be given was “the sign of Jonah the prophet”. In Matthew he explains: “Jonah spent three days and three nights inside the great sea creature, and in the same way the Son of Man will spend three days and three nights deep in the earth.” And he adds that the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment and condemn his own generation, “They turned from their sins when Jonah preached. Yet here is something greater than Jonah.”

The early church took up the image gladly. Jonah thrown up from the sea is one of the most common pictures in the art of the Roman catacombs, painted beside the graves of Christians as a sign of resurrection.

How to read Jonah

Read it as a story, in one sitting, and enjoy its craft. Words are repeated with purpose: “great” (the great city, the great wind, the great storm, the great fish, the great fear, and the “great wrong” Jonah feels); “hurled”, used of the wind, the cargo and Jonah; “appointed”, used of the fish, the plant, the worm and the east wind, all of them obeying their Maker. Notice the questions, especially God’s.

Christians differ over what kind of story this is. Many have read it as a straightforward account of events, pointing to the historical prophet of 2 Kings and to Jesus’s words about Jonah and the Ninevites. Others read it as an inspired parable or teaching story built around a real prophet, pointing to its artful shape, its open ending and its gentle humour. Both readings take it as the word of God, and both hear its question.

In the synagogue the book is read every year on the afternoon of the Day of Atonement, the most solemn day of the Jewish year: a story of repentance, and of a God who relents.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. Most of Jonah is narrative and is printed as prose; Jonah’s prayer in chapter 2 is poetry, and this edition prints each of its lines on its own, as the Hebrew sets it out.

“The LORD.” Where the Hebrew uses God’s personal name, this translation writes “the LORD”; where it uses the ordinary word for God, “God”. Jonah moves between them with care. The sailors at first cry to their gods and then to the LORD; the Ninevites believe “God”, the one name they could know.

Loyal love. The Hebrew hesed is translated “loyal love” in Jonah’s prayer (2:8) and “faithful love” in 4:2, where Jonah repeats the words of Exodus 34:6.

The fish and the plant. The Hebrew says only “a great fish”, and so does this translation. The plant God appoints in chapter 4 is “a leafy plant”; its exact kind is uncertain, and older Bibles called it a gourd.

Numbering. The Hebrew begins chapter 2 one verse earlier than English Bibles, with the fish. This edition follows the English chapters, and the references in it follow the English numbering.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Jonah 1
fields.body_html:
Jonah runs away from the LORD

1The word of the LORD came to Jonah son of Amittai: 2“Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, because their wickedness has come up before me.” 3But Jonah got up to run away to Tarshish, out of the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa, and there he found a ship bound for Tarshish. He paid the fare and went down into the ship to sail with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD. 4But the LORD hurled a great wind onto the sea, and such a great storm arose on the sea that the ship was about to break apart. 5The sailors were terrified, and each of them cried out to his own god. They hurled the cargo into the sea to lighten their load. But Jonah had gone down into the hold of the ship, where he had lain down and fallen into a deep sleep. 6The captain came to him and said, “How can you sleep? Get up, call out to your god! Perhaps that god will take notice of us, and we will not perish.” 7Then the sailors said to one another, “Come, let us cast lots to find out who is to blame for this disaster that has struck us.” So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. 8So they said to him, “Tell us, who is to blame for this disaster that has come on us? What is your work? Where do you come from? What is your country? What people do you belong to?” 9He answered them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.” 10Then the men were seized with great fear, and they said to him, “What is this that you have done?” For the men knew that he was running away from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them. 11So they asked him, “What should we do to you to make the sea calm down for us?” For the sea was getting rougher and rougher. 12He answered them, “Pick me up and hurl me into the sea, and the sea will calm down for you. For I know that it is my fault that this great storm has come upon you.” 13Instead, the men rowed hard to bring the ship back to dry land, but they were unable to, because the sea grew rougher and rougher against them. 14Then they cried out to the LORD, “Please, LORD, do not let us perish for taking this man’s life! Do not hold us guilty of innocent blood. For you, LORD, have done as you pleased.” 15Then they picked Jonah up and hurled him into the sea, and the sea stopped its raging. 16Then the men were filled with great fear of the LORD, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows. 17But the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was inside the fish for three days and three nights.
fields.summary: God sends Jonah to Nineveh, but he flees by ship toward Tarshish. In a great storm the sailors throw Jonah overboard, and God provides a great fish to swallow him.

fields.title: Jonah 2
fields.body_html:
The great fish and Jonah’s prayer

1Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from inside the fish.
2He said:
“When I was in trouble I cried out to the LORD, and he gave me an answer;
from deep in Sheol I called for help, and you heard my voice.
3You threw me into the depths, into the heart of the seas,
and the current swirled around me;
all your breaking waves and rollers have gone over my head.
4I said, ‘I have been driven away from your sight;
still, I will look again toward your holy temple.’
5The waters closed over me up to my throat;
the deep was all around me;
seaweed was wrapped around my head.
6I went down to the roots of the mountains;
the earth’s bars closed behind me forever.
But you brought my life up from the pit, LORD my God.
7As my life was ebbing away,
I remembered the LORD,
and my prayer came to you,
into your holy temple.
8Those who devote themselves to useless idols
abandon their loyal love.
9But I will sacrifice to you with a song of thanksgiving;
what I have vowed I will make good.
It is the LORD who saves.”

10Then the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto dry land.
fields.summary: From inside the fish Jonah prays to God, who answers him, and the fish spits him out on dry land.

fields.title: Jonah 3
fields.body_html:
Nineveh turns from its evil

1The word of the LORD came to Jonah a second time: 2“Get up, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out to it the message that I am giving you.” 3So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, as the LORD had told him. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, a three days’ walk across. 4Jonah began by going a day’s walk into the city, and he called out, “Forty more days, and Nineveh will be overthrown!” 5The people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and dressed in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least of them. 6When the news reached the king of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, laid aside his royal robe, covered himself with sackcloth and sat down in the ashes. 7Then he had a proclamation made in Nineveh: “By order of the king and his nobles: Let no person or animal, herd or flock, taste anything at all. They must not graze, and they must not drink water. 8People and animals alike must be covered with sackcloth. Let them call out to God with all their might, and let each one turn from their evil ways and from the violence they do. 9Who knows? God may yet turn and change his mind; he may turn back from his fierce anger, and we will not perish.” 10When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God relented of the disaster he had said he would bring on them, and he did not do it.
fields.summary: Jonah goes to Nineveh and announces that it will be overthrown in forty days. The people and their king repent, and God relents from the disaster.

fields.title: Jonah 4
fields.body_html:
Jonah’s anger

1But to Jonah this seemed a great wrong, and he became angry. 2He prayed to the LORD, “Please, LORD, did I not say this while I was still in my own country? That is why I hurried to run away to Tarshish. For I knew that you are a God of grace and tender compassion, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love, and one who relents from sending disaster. 3So now, LORD, please take my life from me, for death is better for me than life.”

The plant and the great city

4But the LORD said, “Are you right to be angry?” 5Jonah went out of the city and sat down to the east of it. He made himself a shelter there and sat under it in the shade, waiting to see what would become of the city. 6The LORD God appointed a leafy plant, and it grew up over Jonah to give shade over his head and to save him from his misery. Jonah was overjoyed about the plant. 7But at dawn the next day God appointed a worm, which attacked the plant so that it withered. 8When the sun came up, God appointed a scorching wind from the east, and the sun beat down on Jonah’s head until he grew faint. He prayed that he might die, and he said, “Death is better for me than life.” 9But God said to Jonah, “Are you right to be angry about the plant?” “I am right to be angry,” he said, “angry enough to die!” 10Then the LORD said, “You took pity on the plant, though you did not work for it or make it grow. It sprang up in a night and died in a night. 11And should I not take pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 people in it who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals as well?”
fields.summary: Jonah is angry that God spared Nineveh. God gives him a plant for shade and then takes it away, and asks whether God should not care about the great city of Nineveh.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
And should I not take pity on Nineveh, that great city, with more than 120,000 people in it who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals as well?”

— Jonah 4:11

Jonah ends with a question. God has the last word, but it is not a verdict; it is an invitation to see the world as he sees it. A hundred and twenty thousand people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many animals as well. Should he not take pity on them?

The question the book leaves with you

The question is put to Jonah, and through him to every reader who has ever been glad to see God’s judgment fall on someone else. Jonah believed every word of Israel’s creed about God’s grace and compassion. He simply wanted it kept for his own people. The book asks whether we want it kept for ours.

It is easy to laugh at Jonah, and the book means us to. But it is harder to put down the book and not recognise him. Most of us have a Nineveh, a person or a people whose repentance we would not welcome, and a plant whose loss would grieve us more than their ruin. The book does not tell us whether Jonah ever came round. It leaves that part of the story for us to finish.

Where the story goes next

Nineveh’s repentance did not last forever. A century or so later the prophet Nahum announced its fall, and in 612 BC it was destroyed. But the book of Jonah had already shown that God’s mercy was not meant for Israel alone, and the rest of the Bible follows that thread to its end. Jesus said that the people of Nineveh would stand up at the judgment and condemn those who heard him and did not repent, “Yet here is something greater than Jonah.” He went down into death for three days and rose again, and then sent his disciples, as Jonah was sent, to call the nations to repentance.

Where to go from here

  • On running away (Jonah 1). Charles H. Spurgeon’s reading for February 25 in Evening by Evening, on Jonah fleeing to Tarshish.
  • On the prayer from the depths (Jonah 2). “A Prayer from the Depths”, the chapter on Jonah in The Prayers Jesus Learned, an Ochorus Original; and Spurgeon’s reading for February 26 in Morning by Morning, on the line that salvation belongs to the LORD.
  • On Nineveh’s repentance (Jonah 3). The chapter on repentance in R. A. Torrey’s What the Bible Teaches, which sets Jonah 3 beside Jesus’s words about the people of Nineveh; and Irenaeus of Lyons’s Against Heresies, whose third book reads Jonah’s rescue as a picture of God’s patience with humankind.
  • On Jonah’s anger (Jonah 4). Spurgeon’s reading for July 13 in Morning by Morning, on God’s question to Jonah; Thomas Watson’s The Lord’s Prayer, whose chapter on the prayer’s third petition sets Jonah’s anger over the plant against true submission to God; and A. B. Simpson’s sermon The Death of Self (Galatians 2:20), which holds up the sulking prophet as a warning against a ministry full of self.
  • On the sign of Jonah. Justin Martyr’s Dialogue with Trypho, in the chapter “The same is taught from the history of Jonah”; Augustine’s The City of God, book XVIII, chapter 30; and Jerome’s letter to Paulinus (Letter LIII in The Letters of St. Jerome), on “Jonah, fairest of doves, whose shipwreck shews in a figure the passion of the Lord”.
  • For children. “Jonah Runs Away” and “Jonah and the Great City”, two chapters of Tell Me the Story – Book 3: Kings and Prophets, an Ochorus Original.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Jonah in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

Then read Jonah once more, and this time notice how often God gives a second chance: to the sailors, to the prophet, to the city. The turning point of the whole story is a single verse:

When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil ways, God relented of the disaster he had said he would bring on them, and he did not do it.

— Jonah 3:10
